M.Sc. Thesis · Advisor Meeting · 2026

When Are Space and Time Linearly Represented in Language Models?

Entity salience, language resource, and pooling
M.Sc. Thesis · Yarin Beer · Computer Science, HUJI
Advisors: Prof. Gabriel Stanovsky  ·  Dr. Barak Sober
Motivation

Why we care: a world model you could point at an excavation

The claim we are following up
Recent interpretability work reports that language models build linear internal maps of time and space. A ridge probe on frozen activations recovers when a person died, or where a city is. If that geometry is a general property of large models, it is a free measuring instrument.
Why an archaeologist should care
Dating and provenancing cuneiform fragments is done by hand, from ruler names, script style and archival context: slow, expert-bound, and for most fragments simply unresolved. A probe that reads date and find-spot straight out of a frozen model would turn a scholarly bottleneck into an inference. That is the payoff we are testing for.
But the claim was only ever tested in its comfort zone
Famous entities (world capitals, celebrated figures, headline news), written in English, read out of explicitly marked entity tokens. Our regime differs on three axes at once: the entities are obscure, the language is low-resource, and the unit is a damaged fragment rather than a name. This deck climbs those axes one at a time and reports where the map survives and where it breaks.
The work we extend · Gurnee & Tegmark, ICLR 2024

“Language Models Represent Space and Time”: a strong claim, tested in one cell

Their method, which we adopt unchanged
Run an entity name through a frozen model; save the residual-stream activation at the last entity token for every layer; fit ridge regression (λ by leave-one-out CV) to latitude/longitude or to a year; report R² on held-out entities. Six datasets, roughly 20–40k entities each: World, USA, NYC (space) and Figures, Art, Headlines (time).
Their finding
Recovery is strong (World R² = .911 at Llama-2-70B), rises with scale, and improves through the first half of the layers before plateauing. Nonlinear MLP probes add almost nothing, which is their argument that the structure really is linear.
What the setting quietly holds fixed
Three things at once. Every dataset is salient entities; every dataset is English; and the read-out is always an explicit entity token, a span the experimenter marks in advance. So the study cannot separate the model's geometry from the well-represented slice of the world it was trained on, and it never asks whether the same information is recoverable implicitly, from a whole text in which no entity is singled out. Our corpus varies all three.
And one control it does not run
No random-initialised twin. Without it, a probe's success cannot be separated from what a linear map extracts from any high-dimensional representation. We add that control everywhere, plus a TF-IDF character n-gram floor.
The design

The climbing map: entity salience × language resource

Going straight from the paper's setting to Akkadian changes two things at once, so a collapse could not be attributed to either. We lay the space out as a 2×2 and climb it one factor at a time.
High-resource language (English)Low-resource language (Akkadian)
Salient entitiesA: the paper's cell. World capitals, famous figures, headlines. Slides 6–8.D: empty. No famous entities exist in Akkadian outside these same royal names, so no honest filler exists.
Obscure entitiesB: Assyrian rulers and find-spots, written in English. Slides 9–11.C: the same entities in raw Akkadian. Slides 13–18.
A → B isolates entity obscurity
Same language, different entities. It also asks a second question: is the language itself the barrier to linear recoverability? If a faithful English translation restores the signal that raw Akkadian loses, then the knowledge is stored in activation space by meaning rather than surface form, and translation becomes a way to reach an LLM's internal representations for any low-resource language.
B → C isolates language resource
Same entities, different language. This is what tells us whether the model has learned the actual patterns of Akkadian from the real text, or whether it only ever had access to the content once someone rendered it in a language it knows.
Inside every cell: what counts as the entity, and how we pool
We first run the paper's entity-level protocol, then extend to whole fragments, and pool both at the last token (theirs) and as a mean over the text (new).

Protocol

How every experiment in this deck is set up, and how to read its numbers

Models
Llama-2 7B / 13B / 70B (the paper's own series) · Qwen3 1.7B / 8B / 32B · gpt-oss-120B · three small seq2seq translation encoders (cuneiform-400M, AKK-300M, uMT5-base).
Controls
a random-initialised twin of every decoder (same architecture and tokenizer, untrained weights) and a TF-IDF character n-gram floor. Both appear as rows in every results table, never as a slide of their own.
Pooling
entity last token (the paper's read-out, an explicitly marked span) · text last token (their Headlines read-out, applied to our whole fragments) · mean over the text (new: no span is marked, so the signal must be recoverable implicitly, and it is the only option for the encoders, which have no causal last token).
Metrics
R² on held-out entities, as in the paper, and Spearman ρ, which the paper also reports. We lean on ρ for year because dating is a ranking problem and our year distribution is compressed and unevenly spaced.
Balancing
balanced Monte-Carlo, used wherever the corpus is ours: each of the 8 dense rulers is capped at the same number of fragments and the probe is refit over 200 redrawn splits, so no score can come from one over-represented king. The paper's English datasets are already balanced and need none of this.
Verdict
a score witnesses learning only if it beats both the TF-IDF floor and that arm's own random twin. Beating neither means the probe found geometry that any random projection would have offered.

Two protocol families run through the deck, and each slide states which one it uses in the box at the top. The replication line (cells A, B, C) follows the paper: last-token pooling, ridge, R². The thesis line (the closing slides) uses what the applied dating work settled on: mean pooling, PLS, Spearman. Numbers are comparable within a line, not across the two.

On English the published result holds, and it holds against controls the paper never ran. Our Llama-2-70B lands within .02 of every published number, and the effect extends to a second family: Qwen3 scales 1.7B → 8B → 32B exactly as the paper's scaling claim predicts. The gap to the controls is large in both space and time (Llama-2-70B World .905 against its random twin .170; Art .860 against .029), so the geometry is learned rather than architectural, and TF-IDF is a genuine floor that trained models clear and random ones fall below. The three translation models (uMT5-base, cuneiform-400M, AKK-300M) sit above the random twins but below TF-IDF on English: they are not generically good probes. PLS tracks Ridge closely for every decoder. * = control.

A · depth

Where in the network space and time live

Setup
per-layer ridge probe (no PLS on this slide), all six English datasets pooled into two groups: SPACE = World, USA, NYC (predicting latitude/longitude) and TIME = Figures, Art, Headlines (predicting year). Plotted against normalised depth (layer / total layers) so models of different depth, 28 to 41 layers, are directly comparable, as in the paper's Figure 2.
Reading
rows = SPACE then TIME; columns = last token (the paper's read-out) then mean pool (new), each shown under both metrics, so nothing here departs from the paper: we only add the read-outs it also reports. R² uses a symlog axis, linear near zero and logarithmic further out, so the deep negative scores of the failing arms fit on the page without squashing the 0 to 1 band. Dashed = random-init controls; ★ = each arm's best layer.
Key takeawayThe Qwen and Llama families sit clearly above both the random controls and the encoder-decoder translation models. Where each arm peaks is as informative as how high it peaks: for the weakest arms the best layer is at the very start of the network, which is what "no signal was built" looks like, whereas every arm that beats its controls peaks in the middle-to-late layers, reproducing the paper's depth profile for time under both poolings. In space the best layers are spread more evenly across depth and sit less often at the very start. Two arms are the exception worth watching in the space panels: they track near the bottom for most of the network under both poolings and then rise sharply in the last few layers.

A · dimensionality

How many PLS directions the world model needs

Setup
at each arm's best ridge layer from the previous slide, refit with PLS using k = 1 to 64 components. Same six English datasets in the same two groups: SPACE = World, USA, NYC (latitude/longitude), TIME = Figures, Art, Headlines (year).
Reading
rows = SPACE then TIME; columns = last token then mean pool, each under both metrics. Dashed = random-init controls; ★ = the k that maximises the score; the dash-dot vertical line marks k = 16.
Key takeawayMost arms settle at around k ≈ 16 components. Year is the more concentrated of the two, space is more spread out, but both converge near 16. That is intuitively what the strong scores require: with only a handful of directions there would be no room for a meaningful subspace, and we would expect the weak results the random-init controls show, which saturate by k ≈ 3 to 5 and gain nothing after that. The learned representation is genuinely multi-dimensional rather than one strong axis, a distinction that a single best-layer R² table hides completely.

B · the same test as the paper, on our entities

Obscure entities in English: the date survives, the place does not

Setup
we repeat the paper's own two experiments and change only who the entities are. For time, in place of its famous historical figures (slide 6) we use the 34 Assyrian and Babylonian rulers attested in our corpus, spanning 1132 to 261 BC (Ashurbanipal, Sennacherib, Sargon II), and predict each ruler's year. For space, in place of its world places we use the 25 excavation sites our fragments come from (Nineveh, Babylon, Assur, Kalhu) and predict latitude and longitude.
Input
every name is probed on its own, exactly as the paper does (“Ashurbanipal”), and also inside five short sentences that never mention a date or a region (“This tablet dates to the reign of Ashurbanipal.”). That mirrors the paper's own robustness check, where the same entity is probed under several surrounding prompts. The table reports the name-alone rows; adding the sentences moves the top scores by less than 0.01.
Pooling
name, last token: the activation at the final token of the name, which is the paper's read-out. name, average: the activation averaged over all the name's tokens, which is our addition and the only option for the translation encoders, since they have no causal last token.
Metric
Spearman ρ, averaged over 200 redrawn splits that hold out 20% of the entities each time. Every cell is Ridge|PLS.
modelYEAR  (34 rulers → year)PLACE  (25 find-spots → lat/lon)

Key takeawayTime holds up, and the scaling law with it: reading the last token of the name, Llama-2-70B leads at ρ .701, both families order by size, and the top arms clear their own random twin (.457) and the n-gram baseline (.344). But the margin is roughly a quarter of what it was on famous entities, and by Llama-2-7B (.527 against its twin .473) it is inside the noise. Averaging over the name destroys it: every model lands between .40 and .57 and the ordering inverts, so the paper's pooling choice is doing real work. Space fails outright: the best number in either place column belongs to an untrained Llama-2-70B (.459), so no model beats its control. 34 rulers and 25 sites means 6 to 7 held-out entities per draw, so read the ordering, not the third decimal.

B · from names to whole fragments

Whole fragments in English: a bag of character n-grams dates them best

Setup
the entity is no longer a name but a whole tablet fragment, read in its faithful English translation, and we predict the year it was written. This is the paper's news headlines experiment carried over to our corpus: a full passage rather than a short name, with no entity marked anywhere in it. A fragment reads like “… the palace of my lordship which is in Nineveh I rebuilt and completed …”.
Pooling
text, last token: the activation at the final token of the passage, which is what the paper uses for headlines. text, average: averaged over the whole passage. Nothing points the model at a date, so the signal has to be recoverable from the passage as a whole.
Metric
Spearman ρ and R², averaged over 200 balanced draws that cap each of the 8 best-attested rulers at the same number of fragments, so no single king can carry the score.

Key takeawayThe n-gram baseline wins outright (ρ .775), ahead of every embedding in the table. Pooling matters more than the model does: averaging over the passage adds about +.20 ρ to almost every arm, which is the opposite of what we saw on bare names, because a date leaves its trace across the whole passage rather than at one token. But the arms that gain the most from it gain nothing over their controls: at the top, AKK-300M (.740) and Qwen3-8B (.737) sit barely above an untrained Llama-2-70B (.661) and an untrained Qwen3-8B (.636). Moving from famous names to obscure passages, the scaling law is gone and the models no longer separate from noise.

Whole fragments in English: place is no better than an untrained network

Setup
same fragments and same English translations as the previous slide, but now we predict where the tablet was dug up, its latitude and longitude. This is the paper's world-place experiment moved to whole passages: the find-spot is never named in the text, so unlike a city name there is nothing to look up, and the coordinates have to come from whatever the passage implies.
Pooling
the same two read-outs: text, last token and text, average.
Metric
Spearman ρ and R² over 200 draws that hold out whole find-spots, capping each of the 10 merged sites equally, so a probe cannot succeed by memorising which site a fragment came from.

Key takeawayEvery trained model is matched by its own untrained twin. Averaging over the passage, the best arm is cuneiform-400M (ρ .640, R² .445), but an untrained Llama-2-7B reaches .606 / .463 and an untrained Qwen3-8B .587 / .450, so the reading rule is not satisfied anywhere in this table. As with the year, averaging beats last-token pooling for nearly every arm, and again the gain is shared with the controls rather than earned by training. The n-gram baseline is the interesting exception: it ranks well on ρ (.535) yet collapses on R² (.022), meaning it orders sites roughly but cannot place them.

Cell C · the controls this corpus forces on us

Before we read cell C: what “year” means when eight rulers carry the corpus

Our year label is almost a ruler label: eight rulers account for most dated fragments, and every fragment of a ruler shares one year. A probe can therefore score well by recognising a king's name — a spelling-recognition task, not a chronology. Three devices separate the two, and each one costs signal.

What the three columns do
maximal cleaning strips royal names and titles from the text; balanced Monte-Carlo caps each of the 8 rulers at 21 fragments over 200 draws, removing frequency imbalance; LORO holds out an entire ruler, so the probe must date a king it has never seen.
The verdict, and why every later slide uses these devices
Under plain hold-out everything looks respectable — and TF-IDF already leads at ρ .793, which is the tell. Balanced MC pulls the trained arms down onto their random twins (Llama-7B .433 vs its own random .438). Under LORO every arm collapses to ≈ 0. The hold-out number was ruler-identity memorisation from surface spelling, not a timeline. * = control.

Geo (space) — find-spot R² from the raw Akkadian

Setup
the same whole-fragment embeddings, now probing find-spot (lon,lat) under the paper’s space protocol: balanced Monte-Carlo over 10 merged find-spots (0.1° coordinate-merge), cap 21, 200 draws, StratifiedKFold-by-site (sites seen, imbalance removed) — the space analog of the by-ruler year MC.
Metric

Cell C · what the entity-token probe actually learns

The king-name token is nearly perfect at identity — and useless for chronology

Slide 12 showed the king-name token scoring far above whole-fragment pooling. This slide asks what that score is. Three read-outs on the same probe: can it name the ruler, can it order years across rulers, and can it order years within a ruler's own fragments.

king-name last token — ruler macro-F1 (chance .20) · year ρ pooled · year ρ within ruler

The control settles it
The random-initialised Qwen3-8B reaches ruler F1 .946 and pooled year ρ .926 — matching every trained model, including the 120B. Distinguishing eight fixed spellings needs no learned chronology at all; an untrained projection of the token identity suffices.
And the third column is the one that matters
Once ruler identity is held constant, the correlation is zero or negative for every arm (−.55 to +.20). The probe has learned which king, and the year comes along for free because each king has one year. That is a lookup table, not a temporal representation — and it is exactly why LORO (previous slide) goes to zero.

free-text generation in English, chat models only · reign-dates question: “When did {ruler} reign?” for the 8 balanced rulers → JSON {start_year, end_year} · roster question: “List the rulers of period P” → recall of the target rulers.

chat model answers; names matched diacritic-insensitively against the target rosters.

reign-window accuracy (±10 yr): correct if the answered reign window (widened by 10 yr) covers a true reign year · kings recall: fraction of the period’s target rulers the model names, scored on the raw text (normalized substrings; robust to truncation and spelling variants).

Neither escape route works. Generated answers are far worse than the probe (ρ ≤ .37 against the probe's ≈ .33 baseline, and often near zero or negative) — the models will name Assyrian kings fluently in conversation, but cannot convert a stripped fragment into a date. And prompting moves nothing: across four styles and four scales the probed values sit within ≈.05 of bare, with no ordering by model size. The signal is not being hidden by a bad read-out; it is not there.

Rescue 3 · scale and continued pretraining

Scale and next-token finetuning both do nothing

Key takeawayEvery '+NTP (ft)' bar lands within noise of its untouched base model, at every scale from 1.7B to 120B — finetuning Qwen on all our Akkadian text with next-token prediction yields zero improvement. Queried in plain English, Qwen names Akkadian rulers and their dates correctly, yet that declarative knowledge never surfaces as a decodable temporal representation. The training objective is the missing ingredient, not data or parameters.
Zero-shot, few-shot, and chain-of-thought prompting also produced no gains. This is what motivates the autopsy: if not scale, data, or prompting — then what?

Rescue 5 · non-linear probes

P9 — geodesic kernel PLS: does the manifold’s curvature help?

Setup
mean pool, rows L2-normalized (distances = Euclidean on unit vectors ≡ cosine ranking) · Akkadian maximal + English tier0 (other cleanings in the CSV) · 8-ruler balanced MC, GroupKFold-by-ruler · k=10 NN graph per training fold; out-of-sample through the fixed train graph (no leakage).
Probe
G-KPLS: kernel PLS on the geodesic Gram KG = −½HD²H (Isomap’s kernel; D = graph-geodesic distances), components a ∈ {1,2,3,5} best-a · RBF-KPLS: identical KPLS on the Euclidean RBF kernel, median-heuristic bandwidth — isolates curvature vs kernel · KRR-on-KG: kernel ridge, λ ∈ {.001, .01, .1} — isolates PLS vs kernel.
Metric
Spearman(predicted year, true), best layer per cell; columns per cleaning = G-KPLS | a | RBF-KPLS | a | KRR, where a = the chosen number of KPLS components (grid {1,2,3,5}). λ exists ONLY for the KRR arm (grid {.001, .01, .1}) — it picked 0.1 in every cell, TF-IDF included; G-KPLS and RBF-KPLS have no λ, their only hyper is a. Rescue 6 · supervision

P8 — the supervision dial: how much supervision does chronology need?

Setup
one vector per fragment (average of its token activations, length-normalized) · same 200 balanced draws, train/test split by ruler — the probe never sees the test kings.
Probe
ONE probe with a knob λ that mixes two goals. λ=0: “find the direction that best matches the YEAR” (fully supervised, like supervised PCA). λ=1: “find the direction along which similar texts stay close” — pure shape of the point cloud, the year is never used (Laplacian eigenmaps). In-between λ = weighted mix of the two goals (solved as a single eigenproblem, [(1−λ)HKyH − λL]z = γDz, on PCA-100 features; test fragments are projected linearly — no leakage). NOT the KPLS family: no components “a” and no kernel choice here — the only RBF is inside Ky, the similarity of the YEAR LABELS in the supervised term.
Metric
|Spearman| between the probe’s 1st coordinate and the true year, on held-out rulers. How to read it: if the λ=1 column (year never used) matches λ=0, the year-ordering is already in the cloud’s shape; if λ=0 wins, supervision has to dig it out. ★ = row best. Akkadian shown name-stripped (maximal); tier0/maxking in the CSV.

Synthesis

What a linear temporal world model needs in order to exist

Reading the ladder back down, the collapse is attributable, and the failed rescues say what is not responsible.
Condition 1 — the language must be well represented in training
This is the load-bearing factor. Holding the entities fixed and moving English → Akkadian (B → C) drops the trained arms onto their own random twins, while a character n-gram floor beats all of them. The geometry the paper found does not transfer to a language the model barely saw.
Condition 2 — the entities must be salient enough to have been written about
A → B weakens the signal before any language change, and the n-gram floor starts to lead on time. A linear timeline needs entities the model has read about, repeatedly, in dated context — not merely entities it can spell.
What does not substitute for either condition
Scale (gpt-oss-120B lands mid-pack on English and near-random on Akkadian; the ladder is flat from 1.7B to 120B) · prompting (four styles, no movement) · asking directly · more Akkadian via next-token finetuning (Δρ ≈ 0 at every scale and unfreezing depth) · a stronger probe (kernel and geodesic PLS, and the supervision dial, buy nothing).
And what the “signal” in cell C actually was
Ruler-identity memorisation from surface spelling: near-perfect at naming the king, zero once ruler identity is held constant, and matched by an untrained network. Any world-model claim on a corpus like this must report a within-entity read-out; a pooled correlation does not distinguish a timeline from a lookup table.
The positive result

PLS vs Ridge across all models — the 400M translation encoder wins

Key takeawayUnder the honest protocol, the 400M multilingual translation encoder achieves the highest balanced year-Spearman of every source — above all Qwen scales, the 120B model, the from-scratch MLM, and TF-IDF. PLS and Ridge agree on the ranking, so the win is not an artifact of dimensionality reduction. This is the recommended system for automatic Akkadian dating.
Mechanism · the objective, isolated

The translation finetune alone builds a deep diachronic representation

Key takeawaySame architecture, same tokenizer, same 0.4B size — only the objective differs. Vanilla uMT5-base (red) starts at the random floor and decays below it with depth. The cuneiform translation finetune (Thalesian) builds a representation that rises to 0.41 at layer 10. Training a model to map Akkadian text to its meaning is what instils temporal structure — next-token prediction cannot.
Thalesian 0.411 vs. vanilla uMT5 0.297 → Δ = +0.114, entirely from the finetune. This is the mechanism behind the headline result.
Mechanism · ruling out the tokenizer

Thalesian wins despite the least efficient Akkadian tokenizer

Key takeawayThalesian splits Akkadian words into more subword tokens than every other model on every corpus — it is the least efficient tokenizer. GPT-OSS is most efficient (4.43 tok/word) and ranks fourth; Thalesian (6.22 tok/word) ranks first. If tokenizer quality drove performance it should lose; it wins. The tokenizer is ruled out as the cause.
Contributions and discussion

What we contribute, and what it says about world-model claims

1 — A decomposition of a general claim
The salience × language-resource matrix turns “LLMs represent space and time” into a testable, attributable statement. Cell B is the control that makes the attribution possible, and cell D's emptiness is itself a finding about what can be asked of an ancient corpus.
2 — The controls the original setting lacked
Random-initialised twins and an n-gram floor, applied to every arm in every cell. On English they confirm the paper (trained .905 vs random .170 on world places); on Akkadian they overturn the apparent signal. The same probe, the same corpus — only the control tells them apart.
3 — A confounder-controlled benchmark for Akkadian chronology
Maximal cleaning, balanced Monte-Carlo, by-site geo splits and leave-one-ruler-out, on a cleaned royal-inscription corpus we intend to release — along with the finding that without those devices a bag of character n-grams looks like a world model.
4 — A positive result, and the mechanism behind it
A 400M multilingual translation encoder outperforms every LLM up to 120B at dating Akkadian, and the same-size ablations locate the cause in the translation objective rather than size, tokenizer, or Akkadian exposure. Where pretraining scale cannot build the map, learning to map a language onto meaning apparently can.
Open
Does the encoder's advantage survive leave-one-ruler-out, or is it the same lookup table in a smaller package? That is the experiment that decides whether this is a dating system or a second cautionary tale.
